summary:
Bauchi State stands under two penal layers: Nigeria's national framework and its own Sharia Penal Code, which the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms remains in force, as do the religious penal codes of eleven other northern states. Homosexuality is a capital offence in Bauchi. Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 provide for death by stoning.

A Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men, among them the 70-year-old Malam Haruna, to death by stoning for homosexuality. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard, who told the court that the three had been arrested committing the offence at Gwada village on 14 June 2022. Presiding Shariah judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held that the men violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window; relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Reuters described this as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. Under the Home Office note, a stoning sentence cannot be executed until it is ratified by the state governor.

The Home Office note also records a further report of a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024. It separately records that at a sodomy trial in January 2014 at Bauchi's Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence.

Death sentences in Bauchi have a documented record of collapse on appeal. Amnesty International's 2004 press release states that the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning sentence, imposed on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003. The organisation described a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death had been quashed on appeal.

Gender presentation alone has drawn criminal charges in Bauchi. State police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Sharia penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial before the case dissolved by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Sharia charges for years.

No source records where such detainees are housed inside custody, whether in a male or female wing, a special unit, solitary confinement or segregation, and no trans-specific placement rule, facility or policy is documented for Bauchi.
tangentialFactors:
The Ningi sentence is reported as the first imposition of the death penalty for homosexuality actually carried out as a judgment anywhere in Nigeria, which places Bauchi ahead of the rest of the country on this measure rather than in line with it.

Amnesty International's 2004 release also records a then-pending stoning appeal before a Sharia Court of Appeal in a neighbouring jurisdiction, indicating that the appellate route against such sentences was live across the region at that time, and that Bauchi's quashals were part of a wider pattern rather than isolated.

Two features of Bauchi's proceedings distinguish them from ordinary state prosecution. Charges in the 2022 Ningi case were brought by religious-law volunteers rather than a public prosecutor, and in January 2014 a mob entered the Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court during a sodomy trial to demand a death sentence, which places external pressure on the bench at the point of sentencing.

In the documented case of the eighteen men arrested for dressing as women, the sodomy charges were reduced to vagrancy and the men remained in jail for several years, with the proceedings dissolving only by the end of 2011.

Stoning sentences pronounced in Bauchi require ratification by the state governor before execution, and a 30-day appeal window is granted, as in the 2022 Ningi judgment. Appeals have succeeded: the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's 2003 death-by-stoning conviction for denial of counsel and a defective confession, and Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003.

Custodial placement for trans detainees is not governed by any published rule that the sources identify. Where a trans-feminine detainee is held inside Bauchi's prisons and police cells is undocumented, and no facility, unit or policy specific to trans occupants is recorded.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 Ningi stoning sentence was ratified by the Bauchi state governor or ever executed is unresolved in the sources. A national newspaper recorded on 16 July 2022 that relatives said it had not been carried out at that point, and no later report of ratification or execution is available here.

The outcome of the appeal in the Ningi case, opened within the 30-day window granted in June 2022, is not sourced. Likewise the disposition of the further death-by-stoning sentence reported from a Bauchi Sharia court in May 2024, including whether it was ratified, appealed or carried out, is unresolved.

The eighteen men arrested in Bauchi for dressing as women are recorded only as held for years awaiting trial with the case dissolved by the end of 2011. No source states whether any of them were convicted, released or compensated, and none records the facilities in which they were held.

No Bauchi-specific material on document markers, entry screening, access to facilities, or hate-crime and anti-discrimination protection for trans persons is present in the inventory, so the state's position on those questions is not sourced here.
